title: Contra Epistulam Parmeniani
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa023.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: ego eos ad illa ipsa priora unitatis tempora reuocabo et ab eis quaeram, utrum, quando ille uir tantus episcopus Carthaginiensis ecclesiae Cyprianus de tam malo collegio testimonio liberae uocis usque ad ea scripta quae posteris etiam proderentur ingemuit, erat ecclesia Christi an non erat. si erat, quaero quemadmodum Cyprianus et ceteri similes eius implebant quod praecepit apostolus: si quis frater nominatur aut fornicator aut idolis seruiens aut auarus aut maledicus aut ebriosus aut rapax, cum eiusmodi ne quidem cibum simul sumere, quando cum his auaris et rapacibus, qui esurientibus in ecclesia fratribus habere argentum largiter uellent, fundos insidiosis fraudibus raperent, usuris multiplicantibus faenus augerent, panem domini manducabant et calicem domini bibebant.
passages.english: I will call them back to those very earlier times of unity and ask them whether, when that great man Cyprian, bishop of the church of Carthage, groaned over so bad a body of colleagues with the testimony of a free voice, even in writings that would be handed down to posterity, the church of Christ existed or did not exist. If it existed, I ask how Cyprian and others like him were fulfilling what the apostle commanded: "If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or an idolater, or greedy, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber, do not even eat food with such a one," when they were eating the bread of the Lord and drinking the cup of the Lord with these greedy men and robbers, who wanted to have silver in abundance while their brothers in the church were hungry, who seized estates by treacherous frauds, and who increased their gains with multiplying interest.

passages.original: sed ideo sunt tamquam sincerissimum speculum proposita hominibus oracula caelestium paginarum, ut ibi quisque uideat quodlibet peccatum quantum sit, quod forte magnum est et ex male uiuentium caeco more contemnitur. potuitne grauius diuinis eloquiis accusari auaritia, quam ut idolatriae demonstraretur aequalis et eius nomine appellaretur dicente apostolo: et auaritia quae est idolorum seruitus? potuitne maiore poena digna iudicari, quam ut inter illa crimina poneretur. quibus obsessi regnum dei non possidebunt? aperiant oculos cordis, ne frustra pateant. oculi corporis, et legant praedicatorem liberum ueritatis in eadem ipsa ad Corinthios prima epistula scribentem: nolite errare. neque fornicatores neque idolis seruientes neque adulteri neque molles neque masculorum concubitores neque fures neque auari neque ebriosi neque maledici neque rapaces regnum dei possidebunt. quomodo ergo Cyprianus et alia similia frumenta dominica in illa tunc unitatis ecclesia cum auaris et rapacibus, cum his qui regnum dei non possidebunt, non laicis uel quibuscumque clericis, sed ipsis episcopis panem domini manducabant et calicem domini bibebant, cum idem apostolus praecipiat non eis commisceri et clamet cum eiusmodi nec quidem cibum sumere?
passages.english: But the oracles of the heavenly pages have been set before people like a perfectly clear mirror precisely so that each person may see there how great any sin is, which is perhaps great and yet is despised through the blind custom of those who live badly. Could greed have been accused more gravely by the divine words than by being shown to be equal to idolatry and being called by its name, as the apostle says: "and greed, which is the service of idols"? Could it have been judged deserving of a greater penalty than by being placed among those crimes whose captives will not possess the kingdom of God? Let them open the eyes of the heart, so that the eyes of the body may not be open in vain, and let them read the free preacher of the truth writing in that same first letter to the Corinthians: "Do not be deceived. Neither fornicators nor idolaters nor adulterers nor the effeminate nor men who lie with males nor thieves nor the greedy nor drunkards nor slanderers nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God." How then did Cyprian and other such grain of the Lord, in that church of unity at that time, eat the bread of the Lord and drink the cup of the Lord with the greedy and robbers, with those who will not possess the kingdom of God, and these not laymen or clerics of whatever rank, but bishops themselves, when the same apostle commands them not to mix with such people and cries out not even to eat food with such a one?
passages.notes: The edition's stray full stops (after "poneretur" and "pateant") have been disregarded as punctuation errors.

passages.original: quid enim eis prodest, quod auaros et rapaces, cum quibus cibum sumi uetat apostolus, modo se uel non habere in congregatione sua uel incognitos sibi esse mentiuntur, quandoquidem fuerunt tales in illa unitatis ecclesia, unde se isti exortos esse sic iactant, ut eam in sua sola societate id est in communione Donati remansisse persuadere conentur? si enim dicunt per talium communionem perire ecclesiam, cur eam non dicunt iam Cypriani perisse temporibus? ac sic et se ipsos unde extiterint non inuenientes desinant dicere aput se ecclesiam remansisse, quam totam prioribus perisse temporibus dicunt. si autem in bonis quibus talia displicent semper mansit et manet et manebit ecclesia, discant isti aliquando non sic intellegere quod ait apostolus: auferte malum ex uobis ipsis, ut per schismata conantes colligere zizania eradicent simul et triticum. quae omnia ita disputamus, ut meminerint qui haec legunt uel audiunt, non eos potuisse umquam demonstrare siue illis temporibus, cum recentissimae res erant, siue nunc, cum multo firmiore innocentiae conscientia sibi totus orbis in catholica ecclesia christiana pace conectitur, Caecilianum uel alios qui ei concorditer inhaerebant fuisse zizania.
passages.english: For what does it profit them that they now falsely claim either not to have in their congregation the greedy and robbers, with whom the apostle forbids food to be eaten, or that such people are unknown to them, since there were such men in that church of unity from which these men boast that they arose, in such a way that they try to persuade [people] that it has remained only in their own fellowship, that is, in the communion of Donatus? For if they say that the church perishes through communion with such people, why do they not say that it already perished in the times of Cyprian? And so, not finding where they themselves came from, let them stop saying that the church has remained with them, when they say that it perished entirely in earlier times. But if the church has always remained, remains and will remain in the good, to whom such things are displeasing, let these men learn at last not to understand what the apostle says, "Remove the evil from among yourselves," in such a way that, trying through schisms to gather up the weeds, they root out the wheat along with them. We argue all this in such a way that those who read or hear these things may remember that they have never been able to demonstrate, either in those times when the events were very recent, or now, when the whole world is joined together in Christian peace in the catholic church with a much firmer awareness of innocence, that Caecilian or the others who adhered to him in concord were weeds.
